explanations.explanation: Pharaoh asks, “Can we find anyone like this man, in whom the Spirit of God abides?” That's the king of Egypt saying it right in front of his officials. Nobody in that room asked for a second opinion. Joseph walked in from a dungeon, and Pharaoh pointed at what God had put in him.

Close, but magicians had their turn already. Pharaoh called for the magicians of Egypt to explain his dreams, and no one could interpret them for him (Genesis 41:8). So Pharaoh isn't praising any trick of Joseph's. He says it's “the Spirit of God.”
Nobody in this scene draws a sword, friend. Joseph explained the dreams and laid out a plan for saving food. Then Pharaoh asked about the Spirit of God abiding in him, not about any soldier's heart.

Pharaoh says, “Only with regard to the throne will I be greater than you.” He hands over his house and tells all his people to obey Joseph's commands. The one thing he holds onto is the chair. A king can share a lot, but that seat stays his.

The army never comes up in what Pharaoh says. He puts Joseph in charge of his house and tells all his people to obey Joseph's commands. Then he names the one place he stays greater, and it's “the throne.”

That's a smart guess, since money feels like where the power sits. But Pharaoh never mentions a treasury here. He says all his people are to obey Joseph's commands, and “only with regard to the throne” will he be greater.

Pharaoh “clothed him in garments of fine linen.” The signet ring was only part of it. Joseph walked into that room in dungeon clothes and walked out dressed for the job. That's quite a wardrobe change for one day.
Sackcloth is rough cloth, and that's not what the text gives Joseph here. Pharaoh clothes him in “garments of fine linen.” This is a man being dressed up for his new place, not down.

Camel's hair shows up elsewhere in the Bible. John the Baptist, the one who called people to repent, wore a garment of camel's hair (Matthew 3:4). But Joseph's outfit is different. Pharaoh clothes him in “garments of fine linen.”

Yes, the text says Pharaoh “placed a gold chain around his neck.” That's the signet ring, the fine linen and now a gold chain. By the time Pharaoh finishes, Joseph is carrying more gear than I ever got out of that junk drawer. Gold chain, confirmed.

The text says otherwise. Pharaoh removed the signet ring, put it on Joseph's finger, clothed him in garments of fine linen, and “placed a gold chain around his neck.” So the chain is right there with the ring. It's all in verse 42.
Men called out before Joseph, “Bow the knee!” They went ahead of him in the chariot, announcing him as he came. A few days earlier, Joseph was in a dungeon. Now the whole street is told to kneel.
That sounds like a fair line for the king's chariot parade. But this is Joseph's ride, in Pharaoh's second chariot. The men call out “Bow the knee!”
That would be a catchy chant, friend, but the text doesn't give it. The men calling out before Joseph say “Bow the knee!” Pharaoh placed him over all the land of Egypt, and the call announces it.

Pharaoh “gave him Asenath daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, to be his wife.” That comes right after the new name, Zaphenath-paneah. So Joseph got a new name and a wife in the same verse. Some people spend years on one of those.
No sword in this verse. Pharaoh gives Joseph a new name, Zaphenath-paneah, and then a wife. Her name is Asenath, daughter of Potiphera, priest of On.
Sheep don't show up in this verse. What Pharaoh gives Joseph is Asenath daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, “to be his wife.” That comes right alongside the new name.
The text says, “Joseph was thirty years old when he entered the service of Pharaoh king of Egypt.” That's a long road from the dungeon to the palace. Thirty, and already running the country.

Seventeen is a real age for Joseph, just from earlier in his story. The writer says he was seventeen when he was pasturing the flock with his brothers (Genesis 37:2). When he enters Pharaoh's service, the text says he is thirty.

Forty is a little too far down the road, friend. The text says Joseph was “thirty years old when he entered the service of Pharaoh king of Egypt.” He's got a lot of work ahead of him, and he starts at thirty.
The text says, “In every city he laid up the food from the fields around it.” Each city stored what grew right outside its own walls. That's a lot of grain going into a lot of cities.
Hills sound like a fair guess, but they aren't what the text says. Joseph “laid up the food from the fields around it.” The food came from the fields near each city.
Valleys are a good place for a harvest, but they aren't named here. The text says that in every city Joseph laid up the food from the “fields” around it. Each city stored what grew nearby.

The text says the opposite. Joseph stored up so much grain, like the sand of the sea, that “he stopped keeping track of it; for it was beyond measure.” An exact count was no longer happening. When I count cookies, I quit at about a dozen, so I get it.
Right, because Joseph “stopped keeping track of it.” The grain was “like the sand of the sea,” and the text says “it was beyond measure.” Nobody was writing numbers down by the end.
Joseph says, “God has made me forget all my hardship and all my father's household.” That's the name he gives his firstborn, Manasseh. The hardship was real, and now a son is in his arms.
Joseph never says that here. His words at Manasseh's birth are, “God has made me forget all my hardship and all my father's household.” The name Manasseh is tied to forgetting.
That's the other direction, friend. Joseph says God has made him “forget all my hardship and all my father's household.” Nothing in his words is about remembering.

Yes, Joseph says, “God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.” That's the name he gives his second son, Ephraim. Joseph calls Egypt the land of his affliction, and he says God made him fruitful there.
The text says it plainly. Joseph names his second son Ephraim, saying, “God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.” So the card is telling the truth. This one just needed a True.
The famine began “just as Joseph had said.” He told Pharaoh about seven years of abundance and then seven years of famine (Genesis 41:29-30). And here it was, right on time.

Pharaoh had the dreams, but the words about the years came from Joseph. Joseph told him seven years of abundance were coming, and then seven years of famine (Genesis 41:29-30). The text says the famine began “just as Joseph had said.”
The magicians never get to say anything useful. When Pharaoh told them his dreams, no one could interpret them (Genesis 41:8). The famine came “just as Joseph had said.”

The text says, “although there was famine in every country, there was food throughout the land of Egypt.” Every other country was in famine, but Egypt had food. That's because of the storehouses Joseph filled.
Rain doesn't come up in this verse. What the text says Egypt has is “food throughout the land of Egypt.” Every country was in famine, and Egypt still had food.
Peace sounds nice, friend, but it isn't what the verse says. The text says that although there was famine in every country, “there was food throughout the land of Egypt.” Food is what stood out.

explanations.answer: Go to Joseph and do whatever he tells you
explanations.explanation: Pharaoh “told all the Egyptians, ‘Go to Joseph and do whatever he tells you.’” The people cried out to the king, and he sent them straight to Joseph. That's the same man who started the day in a dungeon a few verses back. Pharaoh trusted him with it.

explanations.answer: Go to the priests and offer a sacrifice
explanations.explanation: The priests aren't who Pharaoh sends them to. He tells all the Egyptians, “Go to Joseph and do whatever he tells you.” Joseph is the one with the storehouses.

explanations.answer: Go home and wait until the famine ends
explanations.explanation: Waiting at home would have been a hungry plan. Pharaoh tells all the Egyptians, “Go to Joseph and do whatever he tells you.” Joseph had food, so Pharaoh sent them to him.
The text says Joseph “sold grain to the Egyptians.” So the grain wasn't handed out free. Joseph opened up all the storehouses, and the people bought from him.
Right. Joseph “opened up all the storehouses and sold grain to the Egyptians.” The text says sold. The famine was severe in the land of Egypt, and the grain was there to buy.

The text says, “every nation came to Joseph in Egypt to buy grain.” The famine was severe over all the earth, so they all came. That's one man with one storehouse system and a line out the door. Not a small job.
The text opens the door a lot wider than that. It says “every nation came to Joseph in Egypt to buy grain.” The Canaanites aren't singled out here. The famine was severe over all the earth.

The Ishmaelites were traders, the ones who bought Joseph from his brothers (Genesis 37:28). But they aren't the only ones in line here. The text says “every nation came to Joseph in Egypt to buy grain.”
